source.title: Superposition unifies power-law training dynamics
source.authors: Z. Chen; Hao Chen; Yizhou Liu; Jeff Gore

page_placements.theme: Training dynamics, feature emergence and representation geometry

record.tranche_reason: The paper constructs a sparse-feature toy network with a superposition bottleneck and tests its effect on training dynamics, an application of superposition to a setting not covered by the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper tests training-loss dynamics under an imposed bottleneck and compares them with a no-superposition baseline. It does not measure feature-direction geometry, polysemanticity, feature recovery, or whether superposition arises spontaneously. The paper reports the fixed-embedding sweep as an aggregate; individual values are not stated in the text.
record.test_reason: Superposition is imposed by construction through a fixed, column-normalized random projection W (K<N). The study does not measure whether superposition arises, nor its geometry, polysemanticity, SAE recovery or feature dimensionality. It uses superposition as a mechanism to study power-law training-loss dynamics. Even the learnable-embedding variant (A.3) reports only loss exponents, not representation geometry. The record's 'tests/T3' overstates the link: no result bears on whether any version holds.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that without superposition the exponent is set by data and channel statistics, α=(a+2b−1)/a. A superposition bottleneck instead gives a universal α≈1, an up-to-tenfold mid-training acceleration they attribute to random feature mixing equalizing learning rates. They note the advantage is specific to mid-training and that results come from a simplified toy model.
record.recipe_differences: This is a teacher-student training-dynamics study using sparse Bernoulli-Uniform inputs, a diagonal teacher, and a fixed random embedding bottleneck (with a separate learnable-embedding experiment). It does not reproduce the original Toy Models of Superposition method or its geometry-focused experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The fixed-embedding experiments vary input decay a, channel-importance decay b, and student dimension K. Appendix A.3 varies whether embeddings are fixed or learnable.

fits_no_version.finding: With fixed random superposition embeddings (K<N), the mid-training loss exponent is about 1 across the a, b and K sweep. Without superposition it follows α=(a+2b−1)/a.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In a toy teacher-student setup, an imposed random superposition bottleneck yields a data- and channel-independent mid-training loss exponent near 1.

fits_no_version.finding: At a=1.1, b=0, the K=512 superposition model's loss falls below the no-superposition theory curve in mid-training, with a >10× larger exponent. It later plateaus at a non-zero loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Imposed superposition can accelerate mid-training loss reduction at the cost of a capacity-limited final loss.

fits_no_version.finding: With learnable embeddings, fitted mid-training exponents are about 1 for K=128, 256 and 512. The loss gain over fixed embeddings is O(10^-3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The unit mid-training exponent persists when the embedding basis is learnable.

record.problems: Evidence is from a simplified toy model rather than LLMs. The main fixed-embedding parameter sweep is summarized in aggregate without per-condition fitted values or uncertainty in the text. The paper does not measure representation geometry, so its results do not directly test the geometric versions of the claim.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for the no-superposition exponent sweep or the general-distribution demonstrations: they report baseline training dynamics rather than a finding about the claimed representation geometry. The paper's structural figures and per-feature loss patterns are not recorded as geometry results.

untested.parts: Superposition is imposed by a fixed random projection. No test of whether it emerges, of near-orthogonality, of a sparsity-dependent transition, or of geometry.
No neuron-level polysemanticity measures. No test of dedicated vs shared dimensions by feature importance.
No study of causes of polysemanticity.
No LLM measurements and no SAE recovery.

record.verdict_notes: Superposition is an imposed design element (random projection plus ReLU/bias readout), not a measured outcome. The study is therefore classed as using the concept without testing any version. Appendix results (β≈1.30 width scaling, optimal K∝C^0.27, general-distribution exponents) are also training-dynamics findings outside the claim versions.

versions.untested_parts: No measurement of representation geometry, near-orthogonality, geometry regularity, or a sparsity-dependent transition in geometry.
Does not measure polysemantic neurons or test dedicated dimensions versus shared capacity by feature importance.
Does not study polysemantic neurons or alternative causes of polysemanticity.
Does not test feature spread across neurons in LLMs or SAE feature recovery.
Does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
Does not measure the dimensionality of represented features or compare 1-D with multi-dimensional features.

rows.subject: toy model (N = 1024)
rows.operation_detail: Fit power-law training-loss exponents with a fixed random projection and superposition bottleneck.
rows.value: α ≈ 1 across the reported a, b, and K sweep
rows.uncertainty: not stated for the fixed-embedding sweep
rows.note: The paper gives an aggregate description of the sweep; separate fitted values for each combination are not stated.
rows.check: Condition ranges are inconsistent with the figures. Section 4.2 states a∈[1.1,2.0] and K∈[32,1024], but Figure 5 plots a from 0 to 2 and Figure 6 shows a∈[0.5,1.5]. The fixed-embedding exponent α≈1 is read only from figures. State is relative to the study's own no-superposition baseline, not to any claim version.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for the catalog claim versions; α≈1 measures training-loss dynamics under imposed superposition, not any listed version.
source_check.problem: The measured exponent is reported correctly, but observed does not describe evidence for a catalog claim version.

rows.subject: toy model (N = 1024)
rows.operation_detail: Compare training loss under superposition with the no-superposition baseline.
rows.value: The superposition loss curve dips significantly lower during mid-training; the paper reports acceleration by over 10×.
rows.note: The paper also says the lower-capacity superposition model eventually reaches a non-zero loss plateau, unlike the ideal no-superposition student.
rows.check: The comparison is against the no-superposition theory curve (N=K=1024), not a separately trained model. 'Over 10×' refers to the exponent relative to the theoretical α≈0.09. Not a claim-version result.

rows.check: Training-dynamics result only; no bearing on claim versions.

relation.reason: Superposition is supplied through a random projection bottleneck; the study measures its consequences for loss convergence.

tranche.reason: Uses imposed superposition to investigate training dynamics; its results do not test V1–V6.

source_check.notes: The source has inconsistent sweep descriptions: Section 4.2 gives a∈[1.1,2.0], Figure 5's axis spans 0–2, and Figure 6 specifies a∈[0.5,1.5]. R1 accurately attributes its range to the main experimental prose.
